item.title: Hackers Hid Vasilek Backdoor in VMware Tools During 2-Year Russian Healthcare Intrusion (2026)
item.description:
A Belarus-aligned hacktivist group spent nearly two years within the network of a Russian healthcare organization.

According to a report published by Russian cybersecurity firm Solar, the activity has been attributed to a threat cluster dubbed Partisan Zmiy, which is also known as the Cyber Partisans.

Known to be active since at least 2020, the group has a track record of striking industrial enterprises and government agencies in Russia and Belarus with a backdoor called Vasilek that uses Telegram for command-and-control (C2) and data exfiltration.

Some of the attacks have also leveraged phishing lures to deliver an installer that simultaneously deploys the legitimate FortiClient VPN program on the system as well as an open-source program known as DNSCat2 that allows attackers to gain control of the infected host.

A notable aspect of the threat actor is their ability to stage destructive attacks with a wiper referred to as Pryanik, alongside taking steps to systematically clear Windows event logs using a utility dubbed Evlx.

The Rostelecom subsidiary said it discovered the intrusion in December 2025, although evidence suggests that the earliest signs of compromise date back to early 2024. The name of the targeted organization was not identified. The exact initial access vector used to breach the entity is also not known.

Unlike other attacks linked to Cyber Partisans, the threat actors remained on the network for an extended period of time without carrying out any destructive activity, marking something of a shift in modus operandi.

"The attacked organization possessed an extensive infrastructure and two-way trusted relationships with numerous subsidiary medical institutions," Solar said. "We hypothesize that the lack of infrastructure disruption is due precisely to the value of this access for further espionage and trusted relationship attacks."

Observed as part of the intrusion is a loader-scheduler service ("vmauad") that masquerades as a legitimate VMware component to maintain persistence and evade cursory inspection. To accomplish this, the attackers are said to have taken advantage of a trusted-but-unmonitored VMware Tools directory location to plant malicious executables or replace legitimate VMware DLLs with a malicious version ("vmtools.dll") containing the backdoor.

The primary responsibility of the Windows service is to launch the rogue binary "C:\Program Files\VMware\VMware Tools\authd.exe" that, besides launching a GOST tunnel every Saturday from 10 p.m. to 11 p.m., runs an updated version of Vasilek (version 1.5.8) once, eight hours after the service begins.

Once installed, Vasilek is equipped to collect information about an infected computer, execute Windows commands, launch and terminate processes, transfer files, capture screenshots, record keystrokes, and escalate privileges via runas. It can also prevent the machine from going into sleep mode, and update or remove itself.

One new addition is the "move_cursor" command that, as the name implies, allows the backdoor to move the cursor and simulate user input on the victim's screen.

"The group consistently invests in stealth and operational security, rather than new capabilities: hostname binding in two independent components, nightly scheduled payload launches, system proxy inheritance, disguise as legitimately installed but unused software, file rotation across the same paths, time-stomping, outgoing message suppression, and anonymous messages on behalf of the group in operator chats," Solar said.

"The backdoor's feature set has remained largely unchanged over four revisions. Due to Telegram being blocked in Russia by ISPs, communication between the Vasilek backdoor and C2 has become unstable."

The disclosure comes as Solar also disclosed details of a phishing campaign that employs JavaScript attachments mimicking business-themed documents, such as payments and purchase orders, to deliver a previously unreported malware family known as HypeAgent.

The Windows malware is a full-featured trojan designed to take complete control over infected systems, packing the ability to steal files, open a console, change desktop wallpaper, turn on a webcam, log keystrokes, launch hidden VNC and RDP sessions, control the mouse, and even deploy a cryptocurrency miner.

It's also capable of stealing cookies associated with Discord, Steam, GitHub, Instagram, Telegram, Binance, ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor, and tampering with the installed Exodus wallet app to inject JavaScript that can collect the victim's password, PIN, mnemonic phrase, and private key.

Earlier this June, Solar also observed legitimate infrastructure compromised by the ProxyCB proxyware botnet malware making automated requests to Russian websites and online platforms, while identifying possible overlaps between the botnet infrastructure and historical activity linked to TeamSpy, a threat cluster known for abusing TeamViewer to facilitate reconnaissance and data theft.

Last month, the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) charged Searzhudin Tamirlanovich Aktulaev, a 40-year-old Russian national extradited from Cyprus in May 2025, for exploiting an online messaging service of a well-known freelance employment platform to send malware-laced Excel attachments to about 80,000 of its users in 2016 and 2017 using 255 fake accounts.

The attacks led to the deployment of two types of malware, a variant of the TVRAT (aka Sheldor, SpyAgent, TeamBot, TeamSpy, and TVSPY) and DarkVNC, to harvest and send data from a victim computer to a remote server under the attacker's control. Thousands of computers are assessed to have been infected as a result of this scheme.

item.title: CISA Orders Federal Agencies to Patch Exploited Plex2Shell, Siemens, and SiteGuard Flaws (2026)
item.description:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added four vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, including four vulnerabilities impacting Plex Media Server that's collectively called Plex2Shell.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -

  • CVE-2026-96652 (CVSS score: 5.3) - Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-96654 (CVSS score: 6.9) - Plex Media Server improper neutralization of encoded URI schemes in a web page Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-96655 (CVSS score: 5.3) - Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-96656 (CVSS score: 8.6) - Plex Media Server external control of file name or path Vulnerability

According to security researcher Zach Main, who discovered and reported the vulnerabilities, a remote attacker could chain the four vulnerabilities to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution. The issues were addressed in Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861 released on August 3, 2026.

The addition of the four vulnerabilities to the KEV catalog follows a report from security researcher boredhackerblog, who found that threat actors are weaponizing the flaws to deploy cryptocurrency miners and proxy malware.

CISA has also flagged two other vulnerabilities as actively exploited. One of them is a DLL sideloading vulnerability in Siemens Software Center (CVE-2026-110936, CVSS score: 8.4) that has been abused in ClickFix attacks using a platform called Romulus.

The second security flaw is a command injection bug in EG Secure Solutions SiteGuard Server Edition (CVE-2026-106931, CVSS score: 8.5) that the Japanese company confirmed as being exploited. No additional details related to the exploitation activity are currently available.

CISA is urging Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to apply fixes for CVE-2026-106931, CVE-2026-96656, and CVE-2026-96654 by October 23, 2026, and the rest by November 3, 2026.

item.title: State Bank of India Confirms Data Leak After 3,897 Customer Records Found on Dark Web (2026)
item.description:
State Bank of India has identified 3,897 customer records containing personal information in a set of about 375,000 records available on the dark web, and it does not yet know where the data came from.

The state-owned bank, India's largest, said in a stock-exchange filing dated October 21 that it "has experienced an incident involving the loss of certain data." The count is preliminary, and the bank has yet to establish whether the data is authentic, how far the exposure goes and what risk it poses to customers.

The exposed information "reportedly included customers' registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, names, gender, email addresses, residential addresses, branch and CIF identifiers, lead IDs, and metadata associated with loan/lead records and other related files," in the filing's words. A CIF identifier is the customer information file number, the bank's internal ID for each customer.

The bank has not said whether the 3,897 records belong to 3,897 different people, or what the rest of the set contains. The 3,897 are roughly 1 in 100 of the records it examined.

Account numbers, balances, passwords, one-time passcodes, card details and government identity numbers such as PAN or Aadhaar are not among the categories the filing lists. The risk in the listed categories is impersonation: a caller or message that uses a customer's name, mobile number, date of birth, address, branch, and internal ID to appear to come from the bank.

The alert reached the bank on October 16 via its threat intelligence provider, CERT-In, India's national computer emergency response team, and the Defense Cyber Agency, the armed forces' cyber agency under the Ministry of Defense.

The bank activated its incident response and containment procedures and engaged an independent cybersecurity firm from CERT-In's panel of approved security auditors to assess what the filing calls "the alleged compromise."

The incident has no material impact on the bank's core business operations, financial performance or business continuity, the filing says. That covers the bank's business, not its customers.

The filing names no attacker, forum or dataset. The figure of about 375,000 matches a claim that the monitoring account CyberPulse56 flagged on X on October 16.

The account said a threat actor using the name Siriusim claimed to have leaked customer documents and personal data linked to SBI: 375,000 rows in CSV format and 2,722 PDF documents, said to include personal information, loan applications and supporting documents, account-opening forms and addresses.

The Free Press Journal examined the listing on BreachForums, a cybercrime forum used to trade stolen data, and found 4 sample records posted with the listing. The phone numbers in the samples were valid. The WhatsApp profile picture on one number matched the passport-size photograph on that person's KYC document, which the actor had also posted.

That check covers 4 records and does not show that the whole set is genuine or where it came from. The samples were mostly loan-related and carried KYC fields, and they did not show whether the data belonged to SBI itself, one of its subsidiaries, or a third-party provider that handles banking applications.

Nothing in the bank's filing ties its analysis to the listing, and the bank has not said whether the 2,722 PDF documents were part of what it examined.

Whether any SBI system was breached is an open question. The filing leaves the source of the data to the investigation and gives no date for when the data first appeared.

The filing does not mention whether affected customers have been or will be told. The bank's cyber security page, last updated in June, tells customers to report any cyber incident to report.phishing@sbi.co.in or the national cybercrime helpline, 1930. That is general advice, written before the incident.

Bank of Baroda, another state-owned bank, told the exchanges on July 27 about a cyber-security incident in nearly the same words, including "the alleged compromise," after receiving "a communication from an anonymous source claiming access to certain data." That filing named a preliminary cause, "potential business email compromise." SBI's names none.

item.title: U.S. Orders DeepSeek Removed From Federal Civilian Systems, Bans New Purchases (2026)
item.description:
U.S. federal civilian agencies must remove DeepSeek products from their information technology systems, along with any third-party products or services "developed using DeepSeek implementations," under a Department of Homeland Security order.

They may also no longer buy information technology products or services from the Chinese AI developer or its affiliates

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin issued the order, dated July 24, 2026, under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018, and the department published it in the Federal Register on October 20. The notice does not define "DeepSeek implementations."

The order names Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co., Ltd., the developer of the R1 and V3 models, and covers its affiliates as defined in federal acquisition rules. The company's privacy policy says it collects, processes and stores users' personal data in the People's Republic of China.

Under the 2018 law, the Federal Acquisition Security Council recommends exclusion and removal orders, and three officials may issue them: the Secretary of Homeland Security for civilian agencies, the Secretary of Defense for the Defense Department and national security systems, and the Director of National Intelligence for the intelligence community.

The DeepSeek order therefore covers only what civilian agencies buy and run. It does not restrict companies or the public.

The 2018 law was first used in 2025, when the Director of National Intelligence excluded Acronis, a Swiss cybersecurity and data protection company, from intelligence community procurement and ordered its products removed from intelligence community systems.

Executive agencies "shall comply with exclusion and removal orders," the law says. An agency can ask the official who issued an order for an exception, and under the council's regulations the request must be in writing and give a compelling justification.

DHS directs questions about the order to CISA's FASCSA Order Implementation Team at fascsa.orders@cisa.dhs.gov.

The order also reaches government contractors. A federal contract that carries FAR clause 52.204-30 bars the contractor from providing or using, in performing the contract, any product or service covered by an applicable FASCSA order, unless the issuing official has granted a waiver.

The clause also requires the contractor to:

  • Search SAM.gov for the phrase "FASCSA order" at least once every three months
  • Make a reasonable inquiry into its supply chain when a new order could affect it
  • Report any covered product or service it has provided or used to the contracting officer within 3 business days of identifying it
  • Send further information on mitigation within 10 business days of that report
  • Include the clause in its subcontracts

An order issued after a solicitation applies to an existing contract only once the contracting officer adds it by amendment or modification.

The Federal Register notice gives no reasons for the order. The signed order is attached to the notice as four scanned pages and is posted on regulations.gov under docket DHS-2026-0628.

The order is dated July 24. DHS filed it for public inspection at the Federal Register on October 19, 87 days later, and it was published the next day.

The council's regulations leave public release of an order to the issuing official, who "May provide a copy of the order to other persons, including through public disclosure." They set no deadline for it.

The law requires the issuing official to notify the company named in an order and the appropriate congressional committees, and to review the order at least once a year.

Before the order, U.S. restrictions on DeepSeek were device bans adopted one body at a time. By February 2025, Congress, NASA, the Navy, the Pentagon and Texas had barred DeepSeek from government devices. Bills to bar DeepSeek on government devices were introduced in the House and Senate that month and had not advanced past committee as of October 21.

China's foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a briefing on October 20 that "China consistently opposes the overstretching of the concept of national security" and that Beijing will "resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies," the Associated Press reported. DeepSeek did not immediately respond to the AP's request for comment.

item.title: Attackers Abuse UpdraftCentral Keys to Plant Backdoors on WordPress Sites (2026)
item.description:
Unknown threat actors breached TeamUpdraft's website and potentially gained unauthorized access to customers' connection keys for UpdraftCentral, UpdraftVault, and UpdraftClone, using them to backdoor WordPress sites.

TeamUpdraft is the developer behind UpdraftPlus, a popular WordPress backup plugin with over four million active installations. The vendor also offers UpdraftCentral, a remote management service that's used for managing multiple sites remotely. A client component of UpdraftCentral is shipped within every copy of UpdraftPlus. 

"Over the weekend of 17-18 October we identified unauthorized access to the teamupdraft.com website," TeamUpdraft said in a statement. "Our team responded straight away and worked through the night to contain it – we closed the access route, signed out every account and replaced the keys and credentials that could have been affected."

As a result of the incident, threat actors are believed to have accessed its customer database, which holds the following information -

  • Names, email addresses, billing addresses and order history
  • Account passwords, stored only in hashed (scrambled) form and never in plain text
  • Two-factor authentication (2FA) settings
  • Connection keys for UpdraftCentral, UpdraftVault and UpdraftClone

TeamUpdraft said the database does not hold any financial information, and that they are handled by Stripe and PayPal. It also emphasized that the UpdraftPlus plugin, along with self-hosted versions of UpdraftCentral and backups sent to customers' own remote storage, are not impacted.

"However, if your site was accessed through UpdraftCentral, please also re-authorise your remote storage and change any storage access keys, as a precaution," it said.

In addition, TeamUpdraft said it deployed a fix to address the underlying issue, signed out every teamupdraft.com account and reset login security across the site, and released UpdraftPlus 1.26.13 (free) and 2.26.13 (Premium) to automatically disconnect every UpdraftCentral connection made before 10 p.m. BST on October 18, 2026, to prevent the old keys from working.

Other steps taken by the developer are listed below -

  • Disconnected every site from UpdraftVault and issued new credentials
  • Replaced every UpdraftClone client key
  • Rotated its keys with payment providers and other connected services
  • Implemented additional monitoring in place
  • Reported the incident to the U.K. Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) and other relevant authorities

Users who have a teamupdraft.com account are advised to change their password with immediate effect (and elsewhere, if the same password has been reused), reset 2FA settings, and exercise caution when receiving unexpected emails claiming to be from TeamUpdraft.

TeamUpdraft is also recommending that cloud customers of UpdraftCentral follow the steps below as soon as possible, since the connection keys can send commands to the connected sites -

  • Log in to the site's own WordPress dashboard, not through UpdraftCentral.
  • Update UpdraftPlus to version 1.26.12 (free) or 2.26.12 (Premium) or later.
  • Disconnect it from UpdraftCentral: go to Settings > UpdraftPlus > Advanced Tools > UpdraftCentral and delete the connection key.
  • Go to Users and check for any administrator accounts you don’t recognise. Remove them.
  • Go to Plugins, including the Must-Use tab if you can see it, and check for anything you don’t recognise. Remove it.
  • Change the passwords for all administrator accounts on the site.
  • If you find anything suspicious, consider restoring the site from a backup taken before 17 October.
  • Reconnect the site to UpdraftCentral.

item.title: PHP2Shell: Two Unpatched Critical PHP RCE Flaws (CVSS 9.2) Trigger Emergency Security Alert
item.description:
This story is developing and was written before PHP's scheduled 14:00 UTC release on October 21. Once the release is out, the affected and fixed versions below are confirmed by the official advisory.

PHP will ship an out-of-cycle security release at 14:00 UTC today, October 21, for two critical vulnerabilities that its security team has rated 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 scale but has not described.

⚡ UPDATE — PHP Issues Emergency Patches for Two Critical PHP2Shell RCE Flaws as Exploit Attempts Emerge

Security researchers at watchTowr say the two flaws allow remote code execution. Only the four supported PHP branches, 8.2 through 8.5, can receive the fix, and no exploitation has been reported so far.

The advance notice followed a leak. On October 20, a post on HN said two PHP remote code execution flaws, rated CVSS 10.0 and affecting versions from PHP 5 onward, would be disclosed on Thursday, October 22. The poster said they had "no evidence beyond 'source: trust me, bro'".

watchTowr then posted on X that the leaked information was real, that the two flaws were under embargo, that everyone had been supposed to wait until Thursday, and that it could not share more for now.

PHP published its notice that evening, at 19:33 UTC, with the release set for Wednesday, a day before the date watchTowr gave. The notice says PHP may release earlier "should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild."

The leak carried the flaws' existence, a score, a date, and two CVE identifiers, not how the flaws work. The CVSS 10.0 figure is the leak's. PHP's rating is 9.2 on version 4.0 of the scale.

The identifiers researchers are using, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, were also listed in the leaked post. PHP's notice names neither. The claim that every version since PHP 5 is affected is unconfirmed too: watchTowr's own FAQ on the flaws says that scope "has not been confirmed by an official vendor advisory" and that no configuration or feature requirement has been described.

PHP says "Full details, affected versions, and the fixed versions will be published with the release." Researchers have started calling the pair php2shell. The name is theirs, not PHP's.

Whatever the affected range turns out to be, PHP issues fixes only for its four supported branches, and records each branch's changes in its changelog. Versions 8.2 and 8.3 receive only security fixes, and 8.4 and 8.5 are in active support. Ahead of the release, several trackers, including Alpine Linux's and security researcher Kevin Beaumont, expect the fixes to ship as PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, the next point release of each branch, though PHP has not confirmed the numbers.

Anything older, including 8.1, 8.0, 7.x, and 5.x, is end of life and gets no PHP fix. If the flaws reach those branches, installations on them will have no vendor patch.

PHP branches that can receive today's fix
Branch Current release (September 24) PHP support status
8.5 8.5.11 Active support until December 31, 2027
8.4 8.4.26 Active support until December 31, 2026
8.3 8.3.35 Security fixes only until December 31, 2027
8.2 8.2.34 Security fixes only until December 31, 2026

Security company Mallory counted about 884,000 internet-facing hosts whose HTTP banner reported a PHP version of 8.1 or older to the Shodan search engine on October 20, 59% of the roughly 1.5 million hosts that reported any version. The count covers banners, not confirmed affected systems, and a further 740,000 hosts reported PHP without a version.

PHP has published no workaround. Until the release lands, the preparation comes down to six steps, most of them drawn from a rapid-response post from Huntress, with CERT-EU's isolation advice added.

  1. Inventory every PHP install, including PHP bundled in vendor appliances, Windows software, and control panels such as cPanel and Plesk.
  2. Be ready to upgrade at 14:00 UTC. Patch internet-facing systems first, and check your Linux distribution and hosting provider for backported packages.
  3. On an end-of-life branch, upgrade, take the system off the internet, or put it behind a VPN or a web application firewall until you can.
  4. Where patching cannot be done at once, CERT-EU advises that you "consider isolating internet-facing applications from public networks until a fix is available."
  5. Watch what PHP starts. Alert on php-fpm, php-cgi, httpd, or apache2 launching shells, interpreters, or download tools. On Linux servers without endpoint detection, Florian Roth's process-watcher logs every program a PHP process starts, with its command line. It sees a program only after it has started and, in Roth's words, "prevents nothing."
  6. If you find something, isolate the server, preserve the web server and PHP logs, and look for web shells, new files in the web root, new cron jobs, scheduled tasks, and accounts.

Huntress said it had not seen exploitation of the flaws in its partner environments as of October 20, had not built or reproduced a proof of concept, and was not aware of public exploit code. watchTowr's FAQ lists exploitation as none reported as of October 21 and the flaws as not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

For comparison, when CVE-2024-4577, a PHP flaw in CGI mode on Windows, became public in June 2024, Akamai saw exploit attempts against its honeypot servers within 24 hours.

The release should clarify what the notice withheld: which versions are affected, which part of PHP is involved, whether an attack requires a particular way of running PHP, a configuration, or a login, and how PHP itself describes the flaws. At the time of writing, PHP had not released the fixes.

item.title: Attackers Hijacked Over 300 Tor Exit Relays to Intercept SSH Connections (2026)
item.description:
Attackers took control of more than 300 Tor exit relays in early October and used them to redirect SSH connections to servers that stole login passwords, a researcher found.

Exit relays are the last hop in a Tor circuit, where traffic leaves the network for its destination. Only a password login to an SSH server made through Tor between October 1 and 5, after accepting the interception server's host key, could have been captured.

The Tor Project began flagging relays on October 4, and by October 5, none remained in the consensus, the list of relays that Tor clients use. At the peak on October 4, the relays carrying the attacker's exit policy made up 7.46% of Tor's exit capacity, measured by consensus weight, according to an analysis of public Tor directory data posted to the tor-relays mailing list.

The researcher, who publishes as kaba, scanned all of Tor's roughly 3,000 exits on October 2 and found 333 redirecting SSH to the same 12 interception servers. The directory-data analysis counts 377 relays run by 59 operators that switched to the attacker's exit policy between October 1 and 4, which it calls "a policy match, not proof of compromise."

How the Hijacked Exits Intercepted SSH

An exit relay only carries traffic to the ports its exit policy allows. The attackers rewrote that policy in the relays' torrc configuration files to allow port 22 (the SSH port), enabling SSH on 342 relays that had blocked it. Another 24 relays that had not been exits at all became exits.

"It seems the attacker is gaining access to Linux based hosts and when these machines are running non-exits they are editing the torrc file and turning them into exits to be able to carry out the SSH attack," the Tor Project's network health team wrote in its October 5 notice to relay operators. Most of the affected relays were already exits, the directory data shows.

The same change closed the encrypted mail ports, IMAPS and POP3S, and on most relays opened the plaintext-capable ones, POP3 and IMAP.

A Tor client only picks an exit that allows the destination port, so these relays stopped carrying encrypted mail and started carrying SSH, Telnet, and, on most of them, plaintext mail. Why the encrypted mail ports were closed is not visible in the data, the analysis says.

With port 22 open, an SSH connection through one of these exits went to one of 12 interception servers instead of its destination, kaba found. When a server intercepted the connection, it presented its own host key. A user who already knew the real server's key saw OpenSSH's warning that the remote host identification had changed, and a user connecting for the first time saw the usual prompt to accept a new key.

In the October 2 scan, about a dozen exits were serving a fake host key, and the other 300 or so redirected through the same servers without altering the key.

A user who accepted the key and typed a password handed it to the interceptor. The interceptor connected to the real server, so the session worked, and every command could be watched and separately logged in with the stolen password to check for sudo and run a base64-encoded Perl installer. In kaba's honeypot, the installer took the same form as the command that put Ebury, a backdoor that hides inside OpenSSH, on one of a relay operator's servers, as described below.

A key-based SSH login could not be relayed this way. Under the SSH authentication protocol, , the client's signature includes an identifier unique to each session, so a signature made for the interceptor's session is useless against the real server. The interceptor could still accept a key login itself and show a fake shell, but it could not reach the real server with it.

A password, by contrast, travels inside the encrypted session and can be read by the server at the other end, which here was the interceptor.

Who Was Exposed, and What to Do If You Were

To be exposed, someone had to connect to an SSH server over Tor between October 1 and the afternoon of October 5, land on one of the hijacked exits, have the connection intercepted rather than passed through, accept the interceptor's host key, and log in with a password. No count of victims exists.

If you accepted an unfamiliar or changed host key over Tor in that window, treat the password you typed as stolen, change it, and check that server for the Ebury signs listed below. An OpenSSH client that accepted the key saved it in known_hosts.

The server that intercepted kaba's connection used an ED25519 key with the fingerprint SHA256:6baCZCPsl+AfQuujUS81fMEE/C7UeJ+AwjrImqmDB3E, though the other interception servers may have used different keys.

How It Was Found and Stopped

Kaba encountered the attack on the morning of October 2, when an SSH connection over Tor returned a changed-key warning. He then used exitmap, a scanning tool that the Tor Project's network health team also uses, to open an SSH connection from one of his servers to another via each exit in turn.

One end checked whether the host key was correct, and the other whether the connection originated at the exit or from an interception server. He reported the results to the health team that evening.

The health team also spotted the policy change through its own monitoring. On October 4, it contacted Zimmer, who ran the Quetzalcoatl relay family, the largest group of affected relays, and Zimmer confirmed the change was not his, asked for the relays to be marked bad, and stopped Tor on the server running them.

Directory authorities began voting the BadExit and MiddleOnly flags on affected relays at 18:00 UTC that day, and the flags were in the consensus by 21:00. BadExit tells Tor clients never to use a relay as an exit.

On the morning of October 5,, a scripted restart swept through 55 of Quetzalcoatl's hosts, with the policy still in place. Who ran it is not known. The directory authorities were by then rejecting affected relays from the network, the Tor Project said in its notice, and the two relays Zimmer had stopped were refused when they tried to rejoin, he wrote.

By 17:00 UTC on October 5, no relay with the attacker's policy was in the consensus, and none had returned as of October 9, the directory-data analysis found. Forty-one relays, nine of them Quetzalcoatl's, were still publishing the policy at that point but were not listed.

Tor Metrics' count of relays carrying the Exit flag fell by about 370 between October 3 and October 5, matching the number of affected relays, and had not recovered by October 18.

Ebury, and How the Attackers Got In

Zimmer described his side in a post-mortem on the list on October 7. Two of his servers were running Ebury version 1.8.3: a management server at Contabo that served as the family's VPN gateway and SSH jump host, and a FranTech VPS he calls Switzerland2 that ran two of the exits.

item.title: The Harness Is the Hard Part of Agentic Pentesting (2026)
item.description:
An AppSec team can point an AI agent running on a general-purpose model at its own web apps with little setup. Sure, the model writes the attacks. But everything that makes those attacks safe to run against production and worth acting on afterward lives in the harness around the model. The harness is where the engineering in AI pentesting sits. The Hugging Face intrusion OpenAI disclosed in July showed what happens when that harness gives way, even inside an OpenAI evaluation built to contain the agents.

Why Each Control Takes Rigorous Engineering

Let’s take a closer look at the attack different stages and the role AI agents can take there

Scope

A pentesting agent makes thousands of decisions about where to send its next request, and the model judges each one against a rule written in plain language. A web app’s real boundary often extends past one domain through redirects and calls to outside services. Enforcing scope means code that inspects every request before it leaves, and OWASP’s 2026 guidance routes privileged actions through a deterministic policy engine that checks them at execution time, outside the model.

Credentials

Finding exposed credentials is part of what a pentest does, so the agent regularly comes across working keys outside its assignment. Which of those it may use, for what, and when a person gets involved are policy decisions that the code around the model applies on every attempt.

Prompt Injection

Every page and API response the agent reads, including hidden fields, metadata and comments a user never sees, can carry content written by anyone who can post to the app. A single product review is enough to plant malicious instructions.  OWASP ranks prompt injection  the top risk for LLM applications and notes that no reliable prevention exists today. The design question is not whether the model gets fooled, but how much damage it can do if and when it does. That comes down to two things: how tightly each action is constrained and which actions require further inspection and human sign-off. Neither is simple. OWASP warns that approval fatigue degrades reviewer judgement at scale, so routing everything to a human simply shifts the failure point down the line.

Proof

In October 2026, Google stopped accepting product vulnerability reports to its open-source bug bounty program after a surge in automated submissions, the majority of which it said were not valid. A finding a developer can’t reproduce is just another ticket to close. Producing one worth acting on means running the exploit, capturing what it reached, and packaging the result so anyone can replay it, all within the limits of the other controls set.

None of this is built once. Every model upgrade can change how the agent behaves, and every release changes the app whose security it tests. And around the controls sit the systems a production agent depends on, including change-triggered testing, routing findings to the developers who own the code, strictly controlling what customer data reaches a model provider, and connecting what the agent finds in the app to the rest of the environment.

Across all of it, the pattern is the same. The model reasons about what to try, and deterministic code decides what runs, records it, and stops it when needed.

How Pentera Apps Implements the Harness

This separation of reasoning and execution is how we approach building Pentera Apps. Instead of letting an AI model send requests directly into an application, Pentera Apps pairs an AI that decides what to test with a deterministic harness that controls what runs. Every action is logged and any test can be paused or stopped at any time. It's the same safety discipline Pentera has applied to production testing for nearly a decade, across thousands of global customers.

The harness also produces the proof. Every finding ships with a replayable exploit script, a CVSS 3.1 score and CWE mapping, so developers can reproduce the attack themselves instead of taking it on trust. Once the fix lands, the exact same attack can be re-run to confirm the path is closed. Tests run on demand or on a schedule, with change-triggered testing in CI/CD coming next, so validation stays inline with development.

The surrounding systems follow the same discipline. Only minimal, redacted data reaches the LLM, with zero retention and no training on customer data, and data stays in the customer’s region. Every test starts with context from reconnaissance across the customer’s attack surfaces, findings from their security stack, and live threat intelligence signals. That context lets Pentera trace an exploit in a web app be traced into network, cloud, and identity on one platform.

In agentic pentesting, the harness determines the results. Pentera Apps builds it in, so security teams get validated findings without building one themselves.

Note: This article has been expertly written and contributed by Assaf Regev, AVP Product Marketing at Pentera. Security teams can sign up for early access to Pentera Apps, Agentic Web App Pentesting.

item.title: PHP2Shell: What Actually Protects You Before the 14:00 UTC PHP RCE Patch, and What Doesn't (2026)
item.description:
You cannot fully block the two critical PHP flaws called PHP2Shell before today's fix, and the one setting being passed around as a workaround is not enough on its own, the security firm that suggested it now says.

PHP will release the fix at 14:00 UTC on October 21 for two flaws it rates 9.2 out of 10, and has given no workaround of its own. Until you can install it, what lowers your risk is taking exposed PHP off the internet or behind access controls, cutting what a compromised server can reach, and having the update ready to apply the moment it lands.

Cloudflare says it is seeing early attempts to exploit the flaws, and has pushed emergency rules for sites behind it that it calls a stopgap until you patch. No compromise has been confirmed, the public exploit code going around has not been shown to work, and neither flaw is in CISA's catalog of known exploited flaws.

PHP has not said which versions are affected, which part of PHP is involved, or whether any setting changes the risk; it says the full details and the fixed versions come with the release.

⚡ UPDATE — PHP Issues Emergency Patches for Two Critical PHP2Shell RCE Flaws as Exploit Attempts Emerge

At the time of writing, that release was not yet out. So nobody outside the group that found the flaws can test whether a given defense works, which is why the advice below is about lowering risk, not promising safety.

The setting you were told to change is not protection

The workaround spreading on social media and security blogs is one line in a PHP configuration file: session.upload_progress.enabled=0. It turns off Session Upload Progress, a PHP feature that's enabled by default, which records how far a file upload has progressed so another request can check on it.

GMO Flatt Security, a Tokyo security firm, suggested setting it early on October 21, saying it could not be sure the change fully addresses the flaws but thought it would help with some probability.

Later the same day, the firm walked that back. In an update timestamped 14:00 Japan time (05:00 UTC), it said the setting alone is not a complete fix and that attacks getting around it are expected. It told administrators to prepare their update, watch for attack traffic before the release, and apply the fix as soon as it is out.

Two people from the PHP project said the same thing more bluntly. Replying to someone who suggested the upload-progress setting might patch the flaw, Gina Peter Banyard, a PHP core developer and documentation writer funded by the PHP Foundation, wrote: "The only thing I can say is that the only mitigation is patching / upgrading PHP. I sadly know too much." Joe Ferguson, the release manager for the coming PHP 8.6, put it shorter: "ini settings won't save you."

The setting cannot be relied on for two reasons. GMO Flatt expects a way around it but has not said what that is. And the whole idea that the flaw lives in Session Upload Progress is a guess: PHP has not confirmed it, the firm itself said it holds only so far as its own research matches PHP2Shell, and an independent code audit argues the specific bug others describe in that feature does not exist in released PHP. item.title: Generative AI Is Erasing Behavioral Tells, Weakening Behavior-Only Detection, Proofpoint Reports (2026)
item.description:
Generative AI has changed what a malicious email looks like. Messages that once gave themselves away through clumsy wording, generic pretexts, and reused templates now arrive fluent, personalized, and unique to each recipient, and the behavioral signals email filters have relied on for years are fading as a result.

Proofpoint shared several examples of the shift at its Protect 2026 conference. In one, a single threat actor contacted more than 30 real estate agents at the same company, each from a different account, about a different property, and in different words, before closing every thread with the same request: join a video meeting.

Federal data points the same way. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center counted more than 22,000 complaints involving AI in 2025, with nearly $900 million in associated losses, and logged 24,768 business email compromise (BEC) complaints with about $3.05 billion in reported losses, according to its 2025 Internet Crime Report.

What AI Changed

Email filters were built for attackers who had to cut corners. Researching a target, writing convincingly in a second language, impersonating a supplier, and producing enough variants to defeat signatures all took time, so attackers reused templates and infrastructure, and that reuse left patterns. Behavioral detection learned to spot them: new infrastructure, awkward language, odd timing, and requests that did not fit the conversation.

Generative AI removes those constraints:

  • Language. Fluent, localized text in any language, with no typos or translation artifacts.
  • Context. Replies that fit the thread, the recipient’s role, and the timing.
  • Persona. Matched writing style, signature blocks, and fully fabricated conversation histories.
  • Variation. A unique message for every recipient, generated in seconds, so there is no template to match.

The result, Proofpoint argues, is that behavior has become a weakening signal. When AI lets attackers make every message look normal, the analysis has to change too, from asking whether a message looks unusual to asking what it is trying to do.

Thirty Conversations, One Ask

The real estate campaign shows what that looks like in practice. Writing 30-plus distinct, plausible property enquiries, each tailored to a different listing and a different agent, is exactly the kind of work generative AI now does in seconds. The opening questions were mundane: whether a property was still open for inspection, what the price guide was, whether a viewing was possible that week. The sender mailboxes were real, and replies landed in threads the agents were already answering.

Figure 1. Different properties, senders, and wording, with the same final ask in every thread.

In one thread, an inspection enquiry sent at 2:58 a.m. turned into a meeting invitation 13 minutes later, complete with a branded template and a claim that the meeting required the agent’s “immediate attention.” The join link was a genuine google.com redirect, so reputation checks read clean, while a parameter in the URL handed the click to an unrelated site.

Because each sender was making first contact, behavioral filters had no history to compare against, and because every message was different, there was no repeated content to match. What the messages shared was not how they looked but what they were trying to get the recipient to do.

AI makes it easy to run this pattern against any business that depends on hearing from strangers, including clinics taking new patients, firms signing new clients, banks opening accounts, and insurers quoting policies, Proofpoint said. A variant aimed at insurance agents used quote requests, neighbor referrals, and coverage questions to build trust before sending a spoofed conference invitation that delivered the payload.

AI-Powered Disruption

AI has also made it easier to run campaigns that aim to disrupt rather than steal. Proofpoint described hostile communications campaigns in which hundreds or thousands of senders write to the same executives, each on a topic tailored to the target’s industry. Some messages carry derogatory language; others carry AI-generated or manipulated images that mock the recipient.

Figure 2. Hostile communications campaigns carry no payload. The signal is the pattern.

These messages have no link to detonate and no credential to harvest, and any one of them could pass for a single angry correspondent. Scoring messages one at a time will not catch them. The analysis has to recognize disruptive intent across the whole set, and read text and imagery together, since the hostility may sit in an AI-generated picture.

Legitimacy on Demand

The same shift applies to phishing infrastructure. One phishing-as-a-service kit Proofpoint highlighted presents a single flow behind four different disguises: a court access portal, a document-signing request, an identity check, and a finance report library. Each page displays a verification code and directs the victim to a legitimate sign-in page to paste it. Because the attacker generated the code, entering it authorizes the attacker’s session, a technique known as device-code phishing.

Figure 3. Four pretexts in front of one device-code flow.

Swapping the disguise is trivial for the operator, so the visual and linguistic fingerprints defenders might match change from one campaign to the next while the objective stays fixed.

BEC shows AI’s effect on context most clearly. In another example, a single email contains a quoted thread in which an impersonated audit vendor and an executive at the target appear to agree on an invoice, a 50 percent loyalty rebate, and a payment date. The attached invoice itemizes audit phases, hours, and rates, and the closing line asks for payment that day to a remittance address that differs from the actual sending address.

Figure 4. A single BEC message with a fabricated thread and invoice. Names and domains are anonymized.
Writing both sides of that exchange and building a believable invoice once took research and hours of work. A language model drafts all of it in seconds, which removes the effort that used to limit how many targets received this kind of attention.

Changing the Analysis: From Behavior to Intent

If AI lets attackers control how a message looks, the signal that remains is what the message is trying to accomplish. Proofpoint’s approach evaluates that objective, whether it is plausible given the relationship and conversation, and what technique is being used to pursue it. The company announced its Nexus Intent-Based Detection Model in September as part of what it calls the Agentic Collaboration Security system.

A bank-detail change request illustrates the approach. The message comes from a known supplier’s real mailbox, inside a real thread, with a clean reputation, and its language is exactly what AI makes easy to produce. Read for intent, however, five details line up:

  • It is the supplier’s first banking change in years.
  • The request does not match the invoice-confirmation thread it replies to.
  • The deadline is tied to a specific payment run.
  • The sender asks to keep the exchange off the thread and deal with one person.
  • Verification is closed off in advance with a claim that the finance mailbox is “mid-migration.”
Figure 5. A bank-detail change request read for intent.

AI can polish the wording of a request like this. But the intent must match the attacker’s path to success, whether that’s the user clicking a link, entering credentials or joining a meeting. That’s why intent holds up where behavior is a less reliable indicator. 

Proofpoint positions intent analysis as a third layer rather than a replacement. Traditional detection, built on rules, signatures, infrastructure reputation, and indicators of compromise, still clears known threats quickly and at scale. Modern detection, built on threat actor intelligence and behavioral baselines, still catches known actors and senders that deviate. Intent reasoning targets the AI-crafted messages that pass both.

Figure 6. Three layers of detection, each answering a different question.

Defenders are using AI here too. Because running deep language-model analysis on every message would be too slow for mail flow, the model is split into three tiers that match depth to ambiguity:

  • Tier one (flash models) evaluates all mail in under 500 milliseconds using machine learning, threat intelligence, computer vision, and language models.
  • Tier two (extended thinking) handles fewer than 1 percent of messages in seconds to minutes, adding sandboxing, topic and tone analysis, and an organizational graph.
  • Tier three (deep thinking) handles fewer than 0.01 percent in minutes, adding multi-stage language model analysis, voice and video, and profiles of privileged individuals.
Figure 7. Multi-tier reasoning: most mail is resolved in milliseconds, and only the most ambiguous reaches deep analysis.

A message one tier cannot resolve moves to the next, and a malicious verdict can come at any tier. The organizational graph is designed to surface campaigns like the real estate example, where AI-varied requests land across one company but no single mailbox sees more than one.

Investigating at Machine Speed

AI has also compressed attacker timelines. Automated campaigns can generate and adapt hundreds of messages in the time an analyst triages one, so a missed detection is rarely a single email; it is often a campaign that already includes replies, sign-ins, and mailbox changes. Proofpoint argues that investigation has to change as well, from analyst-driven, ticket-by-ticket review to agentic investigation that keeps pace with the attacker.

Its Threat Investigation Agent is designed to run one investigation across email, identity, messaging, browser, and supplier activity, map the blast radius, and feed findings back into detection. Use cases include account takeover, abuse mailbox triage, advanced campaigns, false positive and false negative feedback, and third-party investigative requests.

Figure 8. A sample account takeover case in the Threat Investigation Agent, with automatic actions, pending approvals, and an event timeline.

In an example case, an RFP-themed credential-phishing lure led to the takeover of a finance user’s account. The attacker signed in from New York and then Dallas, added a mailbox rule to hide replies, and sent about 100 phishing messages to 42 internal recipients. The agent contained the incident four minutes after the trigger, retrieving 92 outbound messages, deleting the rule, blocking the URL, and restoring the user’s settings.

Four higher-consequence actions, including a credential reset and 14 days of outbound inspection, were held for human approval. The case also lists what the agent could not determine, such as who clicked a link that sat inside a PDF and was never rewritten, and records failed actions, such as quarantine attempts that did not complete.

Defending Against What Attackers Want, Not How They Look

The examples Proofpoint shared point to the same conclusion: generative AI has changed the threat landscape faster than behavior-based analysis can keep up. Attackers can now make every message fluent, plausible, and unique, run campaigns that look like ordinary business, and adapt them at machine speed. The behavioral tells that filters once depended on are disappearing.

A changed threat calls for changed analysis: keeping traditional and modern detection for what they still catch well, adding intent-based reasoning that asks what a message is trying to achieve, scaling that reasoning across tiers so it keeps pace with mail flow, and investigating incidents at the same speed attackers now operate.

Learn more about Proofpoint’s approach to AI, and see a demo, at Proofpoint Nexus.

AI has also compressed attacker timelines. Figure 8. A sample account takeover case in the Threat Investigation Agent, with automatic actions, pending approvals, and an event timeline.

In an example case, an RFP-themed credential-phishing lure led to the takeover of a finance user’s account. Defending Against What Attackers Want, Not How They Look

The examples Proofpoint shared point to the same conclusion: generative AI has changed the threat landscape faster than behavior-based analysis can keep up. Attackers can now make every message fluent, plausible, and unique, run campaigns that look like ordinary business, and adapt them at machine speed. A changed threat calls for changed analysis: keeping traditional and modern detection for what they still catch well, adding intent-based reasoning that asks what a message is trying to achieve, scaling that reasoning across tiers so it keeps pace with mail flow, and investigating incidents at the same speed attackers now operate.

item.title: China-Aligned Bronze Sandcastle Abuses Sandboxie DLL Sideloading to Deploy Backdoors (2026)
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a previously undocumented China-aligned threat cluster known as Bronze Sandcastle that has been observed targeting organizations in Asia and Africa since mid-2025.

"The most distinctive technical marker for Bronze Sandcastle is its consistent use of Sandboxie DLL sideloading," Sophos security researcher Gabor Szappanos said in a post published Tuesday.

Between August 2025 and August 2026, attacks mounted by the threat actor have resulted in victims in the Philippines, Taiwan, Afghanistan, Namibia, and likely South Korea. Evidence indicates that Bronze Sandcastle is most active in the UTC+8 time zone. 

DLL sideloading is a popular adversarial technique that exploits the way Windows loads DLL files, allowing an attacker to trick a legitimate program into loading a malicious DLL.

When an application is launched, it needs to load various DLLs in order to function correctly. If the application does not provide the full path to a required DLL, the operating system looks for it in a predetermined sequence of directories.

An attacker can take advantage of this behavior by planting a malicious DLL with the same name as a legitimate one in a location that Windows searches before the folder that contains the actual DLL. Thus, when the legitimate application starts, it proceeds to load and run the malicious DLL, giving the attacker a way in to the system.

"Because the malicious code is executed by a trusted and often digitally signed application, it is less likely to be flagged by antivirus software and other security solutions," Zscaler noted in an analysis last week.

"If the legitimate application runs with elevated privileges, the malicious DLL will inherit those same permissions, allowing the attacker to perform more sensitive actions on the system."

What's more, the technique enables persistence if the compromised application is configured to automatically run every time a system is rebooted, thereby allowing the attacker's code to execute on the infected host.

Sophos said it observed legitimate Sandboxie executables placed in multiple victim environments, along with a malicious "sbiedll.dll" file, which, in turn, causes the trusted application ("SandboxieWUAU.exe") to load attacker-controlled code during runtime.

Besides Sandboxie, Bronze Sandcastle has been leveraged in seven other DLL sideloading combinations -

  • javaw.exe (Java application) - jli.dll
  • Krita.exe (Krita digital painting) - Krita.dll
  • NvdaHelper.exe (NVDA NonVisual Desktop Access) - NvdaHelperRemote.dll
  • Jcef_helper.exe (Java Chromium Embedded Framework Helper) - Libcef.dll
  • Vmmap.exe (Sysinternals process memory analyzer) - version.dll
  • LineAppMgr.exe (LINE messaging application) - msvcp140.dll
  • bginfo64.exe (Sysinternals utility that displays system information) - snmpapi.dll

"The sideloaded DLLs typically read and execute payloads stored in encrypted config.ini files," Sophos said. "This design minimizes static detection and allows operators to adjust behavior without replacing DLL binaries. Renamed legitimate executables are frequently used to blend into victims' environments, with execution resulting in in-memory shellcode activity rather than additional disk artifacts."

The DLL is designed to load and execute an encrypted payload ("config.ini"), which functions as a backdoor designed to enumerate local network and user accounts, as well as collect system metadata, running processes, keystrokes, and screenshots. Two different versions of the payload have been identified to date: 1.1.5 and 1.1.7.

The payload has also been found to communicate with external sites (e.g., file[.]io, gofile[.]io, ably[.]net, and ably[.]io), likely in an attempt to receive additional tasking from its operators. In addition, version 1.1.5 has been observed using dc.cathaypacifice[.]com and net.dpworldto[.]com for command-and-control (C2).

Version 1.1.7 payloads, on the other hand, have been observed communicating with GitHub repositories ("github[.]com/LatonyCharnleyaW") via the API to download encrypted config files. The GitHub account is no longer accessible.

This is not the first time Chinese hacking groups have relied on DLL sideloading, nor is it the first time Sandboxie has been employed in such attacks. In July 2024, the APT41 threat actor leveraged a different executable signed by Sandboxie ("taskhost.exe") to sideload a malicious version of "sbiedll.dll" and ultimately deploy a backdoor called MoonWalk.

"The threat group predominantly uses encrypted payload and configuration files that are decoded at runtime, meaning that static file-based detections may be ineffective," Sophos said. "Organizations should instead focus on behavioral indicators such as DLLs reading local files followed by immediate in-memory execution, which may indicate decoding and staging activity."

item.title: Google Chrome Adds ClickFix Warnings to Stop Users From Running Malicious Commands (2026)
item.description:
Google on Tuesday said it's rolling out improved safeguards in its Chrome browser to secure users against ClickFix attacks when Enhanced Protection is enabled.

ClickFix is a popular social engineering technique in which bad actors trick users into copying and pasting malicious code directly into their computer's operating system, thereby bypassing conventional security controls.

As part of these attacks, unsuspecting users who land on legitimate-but-compromised sites or click on malicious ads are redirected to phishing landing pages that display fake Cloudflare or Google reCAPTCHA verification or other non-existent errors and instruct users to copy and paste a command on the Windows Run dialog (or the Mac Terminal app) to address it.

The moment a user presses the Enter key after pasting the command, it triggers a multi-stage infection chain that leads to the deployment of malware, such as information stealers or remote access trojans. In an attempt to blend in with regular activity and evade detection, the commands often make use of living-off-the-land (LotL) tools like PowerShell or cmd.exe to download next-stage payloads.

A key reason why ClickFix remains an effective initial access method is that it flips the script on traditional phishing. Instead of exploiting sophisticated vulnerabilities or getting a user to click on suspicious links, it tricks them into opening the front door themselves under the pretext of troubleshooting a commonplace issue.

"By shifting the download process out of the browser and into the terminal, attackers completely sidestep existing Chrome and Safe Browsing download protections," Google said. "To combat this technique, Chrome now detects when an Enhanced Protection user is tricked into copying suspicious commands."

If a user copies a potential ClickFix script, the clipboard payload is scrubbed of any personal information it may contain and sent to Safe Browsing for further analysis. If the security system determines the command is dangerous, Chrome displays a warning. By doing so, the idea is to prevent the attack from taking place before the user executes the malicious command.

Separately, Google is also introducing the following defenses in Chrome to tackle web scams for users who enable Enhanced Protection -

  • Establishing a taxonomy for Safe Browsing site warnings: Suspicious sites, which exhibit deceptive patterns commonly associated with known malicious sites, and Dangerous sites, which refer to sites that are known to be malicious and have a high risk of user harm.
  • Building upon on-device large language model (LLM)-based approaches to flag tech support scams and others, such as fake antivirus and browser update scams.

"This model evaluates page content to analyze key indicators, such as the brand represented, the intent of the page, and a scam likeliness score, giving us rich threat data needed to identify deceptive sites," Google said.

"Throughout this process, Chrome minimizes the amount of data shared with the server by only analyzing page text when a site exhibits high-confidence scam indicators. And whenever page content is sent off the device, it is processed ephemerally – meaning it is never logged, retained or used to train models."

On Tuesday, Google said it's also introducing Financial Services Verification in the U.S. and Canada to validate an advertiser's credentials and ensure ads come from authorized financial providers. The verification program already applies to various markets globally, including Australia, Brazil, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, New Zealand, Türkiye, and several countries in Europe.

"Under this policy, advertisers must demonstrate they are authorized by relevant regulators or recognized registries before running certain financial ads – helping prevent brand impersonation and stopping bad actors from reaching people," Google said.

"Alongside our ongoing work with financial regulators, we're working in the U.S. with the American Bankers Association to use their dedicated registry to verify authorized banks before ads can run. In Canada, we’re engaging closely with the Canadian Bankers Association as we prepare for our rollout."

Apple Blocks Identity Resolution in Safari and WebKit

The development comes as Apple revealed new privacy protections built into Safari and WebKit that block a practice called identity resolution, which turns email addresses into persistent tracking identifiers. The anti-tracking feature is available as part of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS 27 releases.

"In this scheme, third parties (i.e., not the website owner) invisibly collect your email address when you log in or sign up for a newsletter," Apple's WebKit team said. "They send the email address to their servers, create an opaque tracking ID permanently linked to your email address, and send that tracking ID back to the web page."

"The tracking ID is stored on the website and can from thereon be used for arbitrary purposes linked to your email address, such as building a profile of your browsing or targeting ads at you across websites. Logging out or unsubscribing from that newsletter does not remove the tracking ID or your email address stored with the third party."

Apple said the third parties can build more data about users as they log in with their email address or fill in forms containing personal data, allowing them to create an identity graph with their name, residential address, phone number, and IP address.

To prevent this sort of cross-site tracking, Safari blocks network access to identity resolution infrastructure embedded within the web pages, effectively stopping the third party from sending the email address to their servers. The blocking, Apple said, is done at the domain level.

"It's not enough to block cross-site cookies to prevent cross-site tracking today because the tracking industry has not stopped trying to track users on the web," Apple said. "They have ushered into what they call the post cookie era and in our latest releases we have put strong protection in place."

item.title: PHP Issues Emergency Patches for Two Critical PHP2Shell RCE Flaws as Exploit Attempts Emerge (2026)
item.description:
PHP has released emergency updates that fix two critical flaws in the language itself, letting an attacker without an account run code on a web server. The fixes are in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35, and the PHP team says only updating fully protects a server.

The flaws, together called PHP2Shell, sit in the PHP runtime, not in any application, so a site is exposed even when its own code is secure. The risk is highest on servers using Apache's mod_php, where a working exploit triggers the attack before any application code runs.

Both flaws are rated 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 scale and carry the identifiers CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. PHP published them around the scheduled release time of 14:00 UTC on October 21, a day after details leaked ahead of a planned October 22 disclosure.

Researchers at Wiz, Calif, and OpenAI found and reported the flaws, which affect nearly every PHP version back to PHP 5.4.

Who Is Affected

Every PHP installation that serves web requests is at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed, according to the PHP security advisory.

Because the flaws are in the engine rather than in any site's code, even a simple "Hello World" page on a vulnerable PHP version can be attacked.

The advisory singles out mod_php as the highest risk, with a demonstrated exploit in which a single unauthenticated request triggers the attack before any application code runs. PHP-FPM behaves differently, because it shuts the worker down when a request fails early in setup.

For one of the two flaws, PHP's own analysis supports that FPM is susceptible but says no complete FPM exploit has been shown; the second flaw was shown to reach code execution on both mod_php and PHP-FPM, though the FPM path there depends on an operation inside the running application.

An attacker can also read memory from the PHP worker process, which may hold passwords, authentication tokens, API keys, and certificates belonging to other requests, without first gaining code execution.

The researchers demonstrated this reading of live worker memory against applications they did not control, making it independent of the application running on top of PHP.

What to Install

Update the PHP runtime that serves web requests, then restart Apache, PHP-FPM, and any long-running PHP workers. Updating an application such as WordPress or Laravel does not update the PHP runtime beneath it; that comes from the server package, the host, or the container image.

PHP branch Vulnerable First fixed version
8.5 below 8.5.12 8.5.12
8.4 below 8.4.27 8.4.27
8.3 below 8.3.36 8.3.36
8.2 below 8.2.35 8.2.35

PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project, and PHP 8.2 reaches end of life on December 31, 2026. For the older branches, the PHP security team has published source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 to help people building from source or waiting on a vendor.

Linux distributions and long-term-support vendors received the patches in advance, so a distribution package can carry the fix under an old-looking version number; check the package changelog for the CVE, as Debian advises, not the version string.

If You Cannot Update Yet

Only updating is a complete fix. The measures below reduce exposure to specific attack paths and do not make a server safe, according to the advisory.

For CVE-2026-109618, set memory_limit=-1 so applications cannot override it, keep post_max_size low, and enforce request-size limits at the web server or proxy. Do not use RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA as a substitute, because PHP warns they can trigger the same vulnerable path.

For CVE-2026-109619, set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker, and on PHP 8.5 also set fatal_error_backtraces=0. Turning off session upload progress blocks the confirmed session paths but not other variants, and no configuration change fully mitigates this flaw short of updating.

That setting is the one circulated as a workaround before the patch, and the release confirms it was never a complete fix. Session upload progress is turned on by default and can reach session handling before PHP finishes setting up a request, which is why it takes part in one confirmed attack path for CVE-2026-109619 and why turning it off does nothing for CVE-2026-109618.

"The only thing I can say is that the only mitigation is patching/upgrading PHP. I sadly know too much," PHP core developer Gina Peter Banyard wrote before the release, replying to someone who suggested the setting might be enough.

After updating, review your memory settings. The fix adds a new hard memory limit, and reaching it ends the process and stops shutdown handlers from running, so check memory_limit and post_max_size against what your application needs.

If you already patched but suspect an earlier break-in, the researchers suggest watching for unusual multipart requests followed by memory-limit errors or repeated HTTP 500 responses, oddly large PHPSESSID response cookies, and unexplained restarts of PHP workers.

Is It Being Attacked

Before the patch shipped, Cloudflare said it was seeing early attempts to exploit the flaws. "We are seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up," Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht said, calling the firewall rules Cloudflare deployed a stopgap and urging administrators to patch.

No source has confirmed a successful break-in. watchTowr, which reproduced CVE-2026-109618, reported no exploitation in the wild as of 11:26 UTC on October 21, and neither flaw was in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog at that time.

Some organizations took services offline as a precaution rather than in response to any break-in. BambooHR took its service offline across the United States, Canada and Ireland, warned that payroll would be interrupted, and said it did not yet have a restoration time.

In the Netherlands, MijnOverheid, DigiD, the lower house of parliament's site, the national cyber-security center and several education systems went offline, the broadcaster NOS reported; the centre said it had not seen the flaw abused but urged everyone to patch.

How It Came Out

A leak pulled the release forward. On October 20, as The Hacker News reported, a post on Hacker News said two PHP remote code execution flaws, with the two CVE identifiers, were set for disclosure on October 22, on no more than a trusted tip.

PHP posted an advance notice that evening and moved the release to October 21. The leak's claim of a CVSS 10.0 score was not PHP's; PHP rates both flaws 9.2.

The flaws were found by Wiz Research, Calif, and OpenAI's Codex Security team, working with the PHP security team and Google's Gemini team on the fix. The underlying code had been in PHP for more than a decade.

The researchers say AI models helped turn these long-standing flaws into working exploits, letting one researcher do in about a week what they say would otherwise have taken a team months.

Calif, which traced the bug's lineage to PHP research from 2004, says knowing the target's history still mattered, and that current models do not reliably start from obscure, twenty-year-old primitives on their own.

Update: watchTowr Reports Exploitation Attempts, Still No Confirmed Break-In

watchTowr, which earlier in the day reported seeing none, said in a new advisory at 14:19 UTC on October 21 that it is observing "active exploitation attempts" of both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Cloudflare said it saw attack traffic against its customers and watched attackers change their payloads to get around its firewall rules, which it had switched on by default at 03:02 UTC, before the patch. No source has reported a confirmed break-in of a specific server as of this update.

The PHP Foundation said the coordinated disclosure came apart before the release. Around 20:00 UTC on October 20, the research firm Calif mistakenly posted a video of its working proof of concept, and at 07:41 UTC on October 21, about six hours before the fix shipped, the vendor Chainguard published built images containing the patch, letting anyone study the fix while other users waited to update.

Update: PHP Foundation Says a 2024 Audit Found the First Signs of the Flaw

In the same post, the PHP Foundation said a core developer first found signs of the out-of-memory flaw behind CVE-2026-109618 during PHP's 2024 external audit, but a working attack was only theorized and no concrete route to code execution was found then.

Competing fixes each risked breaking compatibility, opening denial-of-service paths, or forcing changes on third-party extensions, and a small team struggled to agree, so work on a fix stalled for months. The Foundation called the delay "a structural failure" of its decision process and its resources.

The 2026 reports from Calif, OpenAI and Wiz, which used AI tools, established the working exploit that made the flaw's full impact clear and moved the fix to the top of the queue. The Foundation said it has since changed how it makes security decisions and added staff and tooling to catch similar problems sooner.

(The story was updated after publication on October 21, 2026, to add later reports of exploitation attempts and the PHP Foundation's account of the flaw's history.)

For one of the two flaws, PHP's own analysis supports that FPM is susceptible but says no complete FPM exploit has been shown; the second flaw was shown to reach code execution on both mod_php and PHP-FPM, though the FPM path there depends on an operation inside the running application.

An attacker can also read memory from the PHP worker process, which may hold passwords, authentication tokens, API keys, and certificates belonging to other requests, without first gaining code execution.

The researchers demonstrated this reading of live worker memory against applications they did not control, making it independent of the application running on top of PHP.

What to Install

Update the PHP runtime that serves web requests, then restart Apache, PHP-FPM, and any long-running PHP workers. Updating an application such as WordPress or Laravel does not update the PHP runtime beneath it; that comes from the server package, the host, or the container image.

PHP branch Vulnerable First fixed version
8.5 below 8.5.12 8.5.12
8.4 below 8.4.27 8.4.27
8.3 below 8.3.36 8.3.36
8.2 below 8.2.35 8.2.35

PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project, and PHP 8.2 reaches end of life on December 31, 2026. For the older branches, the PHP security team has published source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 to help people building from source or waiting on a vendor.
